extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers / mathematicians studying fluid motion and wave propagation (readers of Newton's Principia)
extracted.subtask_description: Collection of propositions, experimental protocols, and mathematical constructions about resistance in fluids, propagation of pressure and pulses, and wave and sound velocities as presented in Newton's Principia (section on motion propagated through fluids).

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental method: determining fluid resistance with pendulums
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct pendulums (spherical masses on filaments) and observe oscillation amplitudes and number of oscillations in different fluids (air, water, mercury); compare arcs descended and ascended and numbers of oscillations to deduce resistances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed experimental protocol: use paired globes of different sizes and densities, immerse pendulum in successive fluids, record initial and final arc lengths and oscillation counts (table given). Use also circular pendulum revolutions to infer velocities. Prefer larger pendula and more fluid trials for accuracy; avoid narrow vessels for large spheres. Repeat experiments, correct for friction at the suspension hook, and account for added weight of displaced fluid when comparing filled vs. empty containers (pyxides) to test internal vs external resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approximate proportionality of resistance to fluid density
rubrics_metrics.description: From experiments, resistance experienced by rapidly moving bodies in fluids is approximately proportional to the density of the fluid: e.g., resistance of quicksilver (mercury) to water found roughly as 13–14 to 1, i.e., near ratio of densities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This proportionality holds for bodies moving rapidly in fluids that are sufficiently fluid to allow free flow; differences in fluid tenacity at equal density (e.g., cold vs warm oil, different liquids) produce deviations. Use experiments with sufficiently large and rapidly moving pendula to obtain reliable ratios; avoid narrow vessels and small immersed bodies which give less trustworthy results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resistance of internal (enclosed) fluid parts negligible compared to external surface resistance
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiment with a lead casket (pyxis) filled with mercury versus empty shows the internal parts' resistance is at most a minute fraction of surface resistance; calculation gives internal resistance about 1/5928 of external in the example.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh empty and filled vessels, account for the weight of enclosed fluid, measure oscillation times/number; if the filled vessel returns to marked positions only one oscillation fewer (e.g., 77 vs 78), deduce ratio of internal to external resistances. Ensure suspension point is firm to avoid error from hook deformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resistance increases approximately in duplicate ratio of velocity (v^2) for wide range; may deviate at extreme velocities
rubrics_metrics.description: Resistance here never increases in a ratio greater than the duplicate (i.e., roughly proportional to the square of velocity) in the experiments described; but for extremely high velocities resistance may increase a little more than the duplicate ratio owing to effects like leaving behind a vacuum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The claim is approximate: for very fast bodies the resistance measured in these experiments is less than for very high speeds discussed elsewhere in Principia; for bodies so fast that they leave a vacuum behind, resistance can approach triple what the general rule predicts. Use pendulum and other experiments to test the velocity-dependence; be cautious extrapolating beyond tested speed regimes.

rubrics_metrics.name: If spherical body moves in a sufficiently fluid medium, the part of resistance proportional to duplicate ratio of velocity relates to densities of medium and body
rubrics_metrics.description: If a spherical body moves in a fluid and we consider only the portion of resistance proportional to the square of the velocity, that portion will be (when compared to the force that could remove or generate the same motion during traversal of twice its radius) in the ratio of the density of the medium to the density of the body approximately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives a way to relate measured resistive force to relative densities and provides justification for connecting experimental resistance measures to density ratios; apply to spherical bodies and interpret as approximate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pressure does not propagate in straight lines through a fluid except where particles lie in a direct line (Prop. XLI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pressure propagated through a fluid is not confined to straight lines unless the fluid particles between source and point lie exactly in that straight line; otherwise pressure spreads obliquely via successive particles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstration via chain of particles: if intervening particles are not collinear, pressure divaricates and propagates obliquely in all directions due to the need for fulcra from further particles. Corollary: if part of the propagated pressure is intercepted by an obstacle, the remainder will diverge into the space beyond the obstacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion propagated through a fluid diverges from a straight track into surrounding quiescent space (Prop. XLII)
rubrics_metrics.description: When motion passes through an aperture into a quiescent region, it dilates and occupies the lateral quiescent spaces as well; motions do not continue purely in straight rays but spread out into the surrounding medium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three cases illustrated: surface waves on stagnant water, pulses in an elastic medium (condensations/rarefactions), and general motion: in each, the motion, upon passing the aperture, propagates laterally into quiescent regions at the same characteristic speed as the direct propagation, occupying the full cone/concentric region. Experiments in stagnant water and sound in rooms are given as empirical confirmation.

rubrics_metrics.name: A trembling (vibrating) body in an elastic medium propagates pulse-motion directly in all directions; in a non-elastic medium it excites circular motion (Prop. XLIII)
rubrics_metrics.description: In an elastic medium, successive compressions and rarefactions caused by a vibrating body produce pulses that propagate as direct pulses (roughly spherical surfaces) with equal intervals; in a non-elastic medium where parts yield permanently, the medium flows into the vacated space producing circular/orbital motion rather than propagating pulses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case analysis: in elastic media, parts of medium alternately condense and rarefy and transmit pulses; in non-elastic (yielding) media, the medium yields to projectiles and circulates into regions left behind rather than supporting wave pulses. This differentiates behavior of sound-like pulses vs circulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coupling of U-tube water oscillation with pendulum isochronism (Prop. XLIV)
rubrics_metrics.description: If water oscillates alternately in two vertical legs of a U-shaped channel and a pendulum is constructed whose length (from suspension to oscillation centre) equals half the length of water in a leg, then the water ascends and descends in the same times that the pendulum oscillates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: the driving force for water motion is the excess weight in one leg vs the other, analogous to the restoring force on a pendulum whose period relates to its length. Corollaries: the water oscillations are isochronous; numerical relations given for specific lengths (Parisian feet) and seconds; changing total water length scales reciprocally with the square root of period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wave velocity related to wave breadth (Prop. XLV & XLVI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Undarum velocitas est in dimidiata ratione latitudinum (wave velocity relates in the 'half' ratio of breadths). Construct a pendulum whose length equals the breadth (latitudo) of the wave: the time of one oscillation of that pendulum corresponds to the time for the wave to advance its breadth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define latitudo as transverse measure between troughs or crests. Use the pendulum construction: a pendulum whose length equals the wave breadth will complete one oscillation in the time the wave takes to traverse its breadth (with approximations because true water motion is circular rather than strictly straight up/down). Corollaries give numerical examples for Parisian measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Velocity of pulses in an elastic fluid is in composite ratio of sqrt(elastic force) and inverse sqrt(density) (Prop. XLVII)
rubrics_metrics.description: For pulses propagated through an elastic medium, the pulse velocities are in a compound ratio: directly as the square root (dimidiata ratio) of the elastic force and inversely as the square root of the density, assuming the medium’s elastic force is proportional to its condensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three cases discussed: comparable pulse distances with differing intensity, differing pulse lengths, and general: when density and elastic force scale, pulse speed scales as sqrt(vis_elastica)/sqrt(densitas). This yields the classical relation v ∝ sqrt(elasticity/density).

rubrics_metrics.name: Local fluid particles execute very short reciprocal motions governed by pendulum law under pulse propagation (Prop. XLVIII)
rubrics_metrics.description: Single particles of the fluid through which pulses propagate move back and forth in very small reciprocal motions; their accelerations and retardations obey the same law as an oscillating pendulum (i.e., sinusoidal/pendular law).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed geometric construction relates successive pulse intervals and small linear elements of medium to arcs on a circle so that the time-dependence of local motion corresponds to pendulum oscillation. Corollary: the number of pulses propagated equals the number of source vibrations; pulses are not multiplied during propagation—once a local element completes its return it rests until excited again.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure to determine pulse wavelengths from number of vibrations and distance (Prob. XII / Prop. L)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given the number of vibrations a source makes in a given time and the space pulses can traverse in that time, divide the traversable space by the number of vibrations to obtain the breadth (latitudo) of one pulse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides a practical way to compute pulse (wave) spacing from measured frequency and observed propagation distance (used later to estimate speed of sound).

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction for pulse velocity from medium density and elasticity (Prob. XI / Prop. XLIX)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given the density and elastic force of a medium, one can construct a pendulum whose length equals the altitude A (height of a column of medium whose weight equals the compressive weight) so that the time of a full oscillation corresponds to the time a pulse would traverse the circumference described by radius A; thus linking elasticity, density, and pulse speed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A geometric/mathematical construction and reasoning connect the elastic restoring force, pendulum periods, and distance traversed by pulses; use values for density and elasticity (or equivalent constructed quantities) to compute pulse speeds. The demonstration references prior propositions linking local element accelerative forces to distances on constructed circles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application to sounds and light; empirical checks on speed of sound (Scholium)
rubrics_metrics.description: The propositions apply to sound and light: sound consists of pulses in air propagated as described (not of subtle ether motion); light propagates according to straight lines in action. Numerical calculations using densities and pendulum data yield estimates for speed of sound, and empirical observations (Mersenne, Roberval, echo experiments) are discussed as partial confirmation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute using specific densities (e.g., air to water, mercury columns) and pendulum periods to derive distances per second for sound; compare to contemporary observations (echo times, measured distances). Note caveats: vacuum experiments reduce sound but perfect evacuation is difficult; use ranges and account for experimental uncertainty.
